content.title: How Marty Supreme lost its grip on the Oscar contest
content.text: Marty Supreme had everything going for it: record-breaking box office for distributor A24, deafening online buzz, and nine Oscar nominations. But then it hit the net. Josh Safdie's table-tennis film, starring Timothée Chalamet as Marty Mauser, a character loosely based on the exploits of real-life ping-pong ace Marty Reisman, is running out of steam — and fast — in the final stages of the Oscar contest. Not only did Chalamet lose the Actor Award to Sinners star Michael B. Jordan on Sunday night, but it was shut out entirely at the Actor Awards — as it had been the week prior at the BAFTAs, where it tied the dubious record of 11 losses without a win. Related Stories The timing couldn't be worse for this late-stage fizzle, against the backdrop of final Academy Awards voting, which began Feb. 26 and ends March 5. So where did the Marty Supreme Oscar campaign go off the rails, and can it be saved before it's too late? Paddles up! Let's dive in. 1. Josh Safdie Drama Kylie Jenner, Timothée Chalamet, and Josh Safdie at the 2026 Golden GlobesChristopher Polk/2026GG/Penske Media On Jan. 26, four days following the Oscar nominations, Page Six Hollywood, the gossip site of the newly launched California Post, alleged that Safdie oversaw a toxic and unsafe environment on a previous film set. According to the tabloid, which led with the story on its front page, Josh and his filmmaker brother, Benny Safdie, parted ways in 2023 after the latter "learned the full scope of the events" that occurred during the filming of their 2017 film Good Time. Anonymous sources were quoted saying that "a 17-year-old girl was cast to play a prostitute in the crime thriller. Once on set, the teenager was thrust into a scene that involved nudity and simulated sex." The allegations in the unconfirmed piece, which many in the industry saw as part of a potential smear campaign to take down Marty Supreme (in the vein of last year's Emilia Pérez scandal), were then widely amplified in other outlets and on social media. Safdie, who is nominated for four Oscars this year as a producer, director, writer, and editor, took home prizes at various critics' groups (including New York and Los Angeles) before the Page Six story broke, but hasn't scored anything since. At first, it appeared that Chalamet was insulated from the allegations, but while the actor prevailed at the Critics Choice and Golden Globes before the controversy, he has come up empty-handed afterward. 2. Confusing Promo Tour 'Marty Supreme' orange blimpVariety The Marty Supreme campaigners took a lot of strategic gambles while promoting the film, and while some of them worked — like the notorious orange blimp — others served only to confuse voters. At the start of awards season in mid-November, an enormous blimp soared over Hollywood, plus various cities in New Mexico and Texas. Fans immediately likened the airship to the orange Nickelodeon Kids' Choice Awards blimp. The film's marketing team sent orange ping-pong balls to members of the press, a callback to one of the film's storylines. And Chalamet collaborated with clothing brand Nahmias to design original athletic gear that launched a social media craze featuring celebs in orange hoodies. Timothée Chalamet in Doni Nahmias tracksuitMatthew Kavanagh/A24 Now for the bad. The blimp concept originated from a Zoom video for a fake, meta Marty Supreme marketing campaign. Praised by Gen Z, and panned by their elders, the 18-minute tongue-in-cheek sketch featured Chalamet pitching ideas to his team for how to promote the movie, including painting the Statue of Liberty orange. A much-memed excerpt involved the actor shouting "Schwap!" every time he wanted to accentuate a point. It may all prove to be too awkward for older-skewing Oscar voters to forget. 3. Greatness Overload While the faux marketing video was making the rounds, Chalamet was appearing on talk shows seemingly in character as the despicable Marty Mauser. "This is probably my best performance," he said in what could only be described as taking Method acting to the extreme. "It's been seven, eight years that I feel like I've been handing in really, really committed, top-of-the-line performances. ... This is really some top-level sh-t." Chalamet's non-humble campaigning persona for Marty Supreme harkened back to when he won the Actor Award the year prior for A Complete Unknown, declaring at the podium he was in "pursuit of greatness," and that he wanted to be "one of the greats" within the acting industry. Once the film had successfully launched in theaters, however, he downshifted to a more humble campaign approach, with heartfelt acceptance speeches at the Palm Springs Film Festival and the Critics Choice Awards, thanking Safdie for telling a story about a "relatable dream" as well as his "partner of three years, Kylie Jenner, "I couldn't do this without you," he said from the stage. 4. Shark Bite Kevin O'Leary at the 2026 Actor Awards wearing an autographed Michael Jordan-Kobe Bryant basketball card as a necklace supposedly worth $19MGilbert Flores/Variety Kevin O'Leary was an out-of-the-box choice to play Milton Rockwell, a businessman who takes an interest in Marty. The multimillionaire, nicknamed "Mr. Wonderful," won an Emmy for producing Shark Tank, and recently shared in Marty Supreme's Actor Award nomination for Best Film Ensemble. But he comes with a lot of political baggage. O'Leary is an unapologetic fan of the current presidential administration, and regularly trashes Democrats, the favored party of liberal Hollywood, on cable news. On Jan. 28, as Oscar season was ramping up, O'Leary and Nicki Minaj, another polarizing media figure, stood shoulder-to-shoulder with Donald Trump. "Kevin is so nice," the president declared. "He's with me 90 percent of the time, but when he's with me, he's really with me great." Those optics were not ideal for A24 Oscar campaigners trying to sell the movie to left-leaning Academy voters. When Safdie was trying to convince O'Leary to play the film's pen tycoon, the director allegedly declared, "We're looking for a real a--hole, and you're it," according to Vanity Fair. Amazingly, that was not the first time the entrepreneur had heard those words, as Mark Burnett's production company told him the same thing 17 years earlier when they were searching for a villain for Shark Tank. 5. Precursor Shut-Outs Timothée Chalamet at the 2026 BAFTA AwardsJames McCauley/Variety At the end of the day, the thing that matters most at the Oscars is momentum: Voters want to be on the winning team. Films like Sinners, One Battle After Another, and Frankenstein continue to stack guild prizes on the road to the big day, while Marty Supreme has stalled. Outside of a victory at the Guild of Music Supervisors Awards (for which there is no corresponding Oscar category), Marty hasn't won at any recent precursor. In fact, Marty Supreme recently set a record for losing. At the BAFTA Awards, the film experienced a historic 0-for-11 shut-out, tying Women in Love (1969) and Finding Neverland (2004). Both of those films, however, still took home Oscars: Best Actress for Glenda Jackson for the former, and Best Score for Jan A.P. Kaczmarek for the latter. With a few more guild awards to come, including the Writers Guild and the American Society of Cinematographers next weekend, Marty Supreme still has a chance to get on the board. In the Gold Derby data, Chalamet is currently still out front to win the Best Actor Oscar, but he's falling fast to Jordan. Of course, it's not too late for Chalamet. He received a blimp-load of support for the film, with many critics hailing it as the strongest performance of his career. If enough Oscar voters still feel the same way, it's easy to envisage "Timmy" taking the stage when it matters most. Oscars 2026ContenderOdds 1.Michael B. Jordan 63.0% 2.Timothée Chalamet 25.4% 3.Wagner Moura 7.5% 4.Leonardo DiCaprio 3.1% 5.Ethan Hawke 0.9% As for its other eight categories, Marty Supreme places third for original screenplay; fourth for casting, costume design, film editing, and production design; fifth for director and cinematography; and seventh for picture. Find out who wins when the 2026 Oscars air March 15 on ABC.
